activities.anchor: The system runs on two engines
activities.caption: file the jobs — gallery, auction house or museum?
activities.name: ammEnginesBuckets

config.prompt: Three institutions climb one value chain. File each job:

items.label: sells work for the first time
invests in careers — stipends, exhibitions, price-building
allocates to 'the best collectors, not the biggest cheque'
resells — record nights that set public prices
fees near 15–25%, guarantees underwriting the theatre
converts scholarship and display into legitimacy
holds the scarce resource the market cannot manufacture

config.why: Galleries build a career before they sell it; auctions resell and manufacture public prices; museums mint the legitimacy both engines feed on. Same loop, three machines.

activities.caption: pair each instrument with its testimony
activities.name: ammForensicsMatch

config.prompt: The object is testimony. Pair each instrument with what it reveals:

pairs.left: titanium white in the paint layer
pairs.right: a date after ~1921 — self-refuting for a 'Renaissance' work
the felling date of the oak panel itself
an age that develops like tree rings

config.why: Material evidence wins: pigments date the paint from the inside out, panels from their rings — the lesson van Meegeren forced on the connoisseur's eye.

activities.anchor: fooled the director of Museum Boijmans
activities.caption: rebuild the van Meegeren case, in order
activities.name: ammVMeegerenOrder

config.prompt: The scam that criminal charges cracked — put the case in order:
items: 1937 — the fake Vermeer 'The Supper at Emmaus' fools the director of Museum Boijmans
wartime — a 'Vermeer' is sold to Göring
after the war — the sale makes van Meegeren a traitor
1945–47 — he demonstrates by painting another fake under supervision
config.why: Nothing visual exposed him: only a criminal charge did. The field had to admit that connoisseur eye and material evidence can disagree — and that material evidence wins.

activities.anchor: the crowd is the business model
activities.caption: call the magnitude — the Louvre's daily tide
activities.name: ammLouvreEstimate

config.prompt: The Louvre receives roughly eight to ten million visitors a year. Roughly how many is that per day?
config.why: Nine million ÷ 365 ≈ 25,000 a day — the crowd is the business model, which is why the gift shop, café and ticketing analytics are the institution's actual economics.
config.context: The Tutankhamun tour of 1976–79 drew on the order of eight million visitors in total across seven American cities.

activities.anchor: and trust is its only non-renewable resource
activities.caption: run the museum — three doors, one trust engine
activities.name: ammGovernanceBranch

config.root: You run a mid-size museum. Budget crisis. The board wants a decision today.

start.text: The deficit is real. Choose a door:

choices.label: Sell three works from the collection to cover salaries
choices.feedback: The finance committee beams; the head of collections goes pale.

choices.label: Accept a £1 million naming gift from a family under activist pressure
choices.feedback: The gift committee smiles; the campaigns team does not.

choices.label: Program a Tutankhamun-scale blockbuster for next summer
choices.feedback: Marketing doubles its budget; curators start negotiating loans.

deaccession.text: Professional codes limit deaccession proceeds to acquisitions and direct care of the collection — covering salaries with them is precisely the violation that turns a budget fix into a scandal.

naming.text: Donors' reputations can become the institution's liability: the National Portrait Gallery declined £1M in 2018, the Guggenheim refused further Sackler money in 2019, and the Met removed the family's name from its wing in 2021.

blockbuster.text: Since the 1976–79 Tutankhamun tour drew ~8 million visitors, museums have known art can be programmed like cinema — and whatever the blockbuster shows tours with the institution's canonising stamp on it.

config.why: Every door spends or builds the same resource: trust — the museum's only non-renewable resource.

activities.caption: pin the transfer on the provenance clock
activities.name: ammBeninPlace

config.prompt: In what year did Germany formally transfer ownership of more than a thousand Benin objects to Nigeria?
config.why: 2022 — 125 years after the 1897 punitive expedition burned Benin City, and the same year the Smithsonian returned 29 objects: provenance histories can reverse decades of 'universal museum' policy.
config.context: The British Museum still holds on the order of 900 Benin objects; Greece has formally requested the Parthenon Marbles since 1983.

activities.caption: which demand curve is a Veblen good?
activities.name: ammVeblenTrace

config.prompt: The art market prices belief and status, not cash flow. Which demand curve belongs to a Veblen good — the one where demand can RISE with price?
config.why: For a Veblen good the price itself advertises the owner, so the curve slopes up — taste functioning as class capital, drawn in two lines.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — reading an auction result
activities.name: ammAuctionSpot

config.prompt: This auction-night summary contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: The house publishes an estimate band; the reserve sits inside it.
A guarantee is a pre-arranged floor — a third party has underwritten the minimum.
Chandelier bidding is legal in New York up to the reserve.
The hammer falls at $400M, so the buyer pays exactly $400M — hammer price is the final price.
Salvator Mundi's $450.3M headline was a $400M hammer plus about $50M of fees.
config.correction: The hammer is NOT the final price — the buyer's premium, a sliding fee that starts near a quarter of the hammer, sits on top.
config.why: The premium is why a $400M hammer became a $450.3M headline: the theatre is part of the valuation, and the invoice knows it.
